When the leader says OK, the patrol pulls the PL back. The back Scout coils the rope as it comes, ready for the next throw.
Untie the knot. The PL goes to the back. The next Scout takes the tyre and mat, and the next throws.
When everyone has done both jobs, the patrol stands to attention with the rope coiled on the tyre on the mat. The fastest wins.

blocks.heading: Tips
items: A very good time is 10 to 15 seconds per Scout.
Use it at the start, middle and end of a Patrol Leaders' course to see how much each patrol improves.

blocks.text: From Belmont Scouts' games folders; the original author is not known.
Everyone stands on one sheet of paper. Fold it, and stand on it again, and again.

items.item: Sheet of newspaper or flipchart paper per team

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Teams of five or six stand on their sheet. Shoes can come off if inside.
Everyone steps off. Fold the sheet in half.
Everyone steps back on.
Keep folding. The last team with everyone still on the paper wins.

blocks.heading: Variations
items: Standing on one leg, or other balancing tricks, are allowed and encouraged.

blocks.text: Based on a game in MacScouter's Great Games Resource (macscouter.com).

title: Trust Falls
cast: Pairs or groups · hall or field

blocks.text: Fall backwards and let your partner catch you.

blocks.heading: Safety
items: Only for older Scouts, with an adult watching every group. The catchers keep a wide stance, with one foot forward and arms ready.
Never let anyone try it on their own. Stop the activity if there is any messing about.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: One Scout, the faller, stands with their back to a partner. The partner stands close behind them, with arms up and one leg forward.
The faller crosses their arms, keeps their body straight, and falls backwards. The catcher catches them under the shoulders.
Swap places. Try a larger distance only once everyone is confident.
Another version has two Scouts face each other with hands out, and fall towards each other.

blocks.text: Based on a game in MacScouter's Great Games Resource (macscouter.com).
A Scout in the middle falls in any direction, and the circle catches them and stands them up.

blocks.heading: Safety
items: Older Scouts only, with an adult watching. Everyone in the circle stands in a strong stance with hands up.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: The group stands close in a circle, shoulder to shoulder. One Scout stands in the middle with arms crossed and body straight.
The Scout falls slowly in any direction. The circle catches them and gently passes them back upright.
Swap until everyone has had a turn.

blocks.text: Based on a game in MacScouter's Great Games Resource (macscouter.com).
With eyes closed, form a square or triangle using a rope.

items.item: Long rope, tied into a loop

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Everyone holds the rope, then closes their eyes or puts on a blindfold.
Everyone puts the rope on the floor and walks a few steps away, then walks back.
Without taking blindfolds off, the group must form a shape with the rope, such as a square or a triangle.
To make it harder, tell some Scouts to stay silent.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask afterwards
items: Who led? How did you share ideas?
How did you trust each other?

blocks.text: Based on a game in MacScouter's Great Games Resource (macscouter.com). Blind Shapes and "The Perfect Square" were the same game.

title: Robots
cast: 3 to 5 per team · hall or field

blocks.text: A blindfolded "robot" is guided by two teammates, one who can only see and one who can only talk.

items.item: "Bomb" to fetch, such as a mini football

blocks.heading: Safety
items: A leader watches every robot and stops anyone who steps out of the area.

blocks.heading: The three roles
items: **Robot:** blindfolded, facing the bomb, and the only person allowed in the area.
**Communicator:** faces away from the area and must never look at the robot.
**Observer:** faces the area and watches the robot, but cannot speak at all.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Divide into teams of three to five and give each team a role each.
The observer shows the communicator what to say using signs, and the communicator calls instructions to the robot.
The first robot to retrieve the bomb for their team wins.
Rotate roles every three minutes, so everyone gets to be the robot.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask afterwards
items: Did you have a plan, and did you change it?
How did it feel being blindfolded? Did you trust your communicator?
What would you change?

blocks.text: From Belmont Scouts' games folders; the original author is not known. Three identical copies were in the folders under different names, including "Tui Game".
A patrol forms a living amoeba and moves through a field under the direction of its "nucleus".

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Each amoeba has three parts. The cell wall is made of Scouts who face outward, link elbows and wear blindfolds. They cannot talk.
The protoplasm is a group of Scouts inside the wall, who cannot talk either.
The nucleus sits on the shoulders of a couple of the protoplasm, and is the only one who can speak. They can see.
The amoeba travels out to a marker and back, guided by the nucleus.
Score by time: the shortest out-and-back time wins.

blocks.heading: Safety
items: Check the route first. Leaders walk beside each amoeba.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game. From a team-building night in 2018.
Every Scout gets a limitation by drawing a card, and the patrol must help each other round a course.

items.item: Obstacle course, roped off, about 1.2 m wide

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Each Scout draws a card. Clubs means no legs (tie ankles together), spades no arms (hands tied behind), hearts no talking (a loose scarf over the mouth), diamonds no sight (blindfold).
The patrol must get everyone round the track, helping one another.
The shortest time wins.

blocks.text: This game uses disability as a theme. Think carefully before you play it, and reword it to be about "limits" for a mixed group.
A Belmont Scouts game. From a team-building night in 2018.
Lower a light pole to the ground, with every finger staying on it.

items.item: Light pole, about 2 m long, such as thin plastic tube or bamboo

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Patrols stand in two rows facing each other. Everyone holds out an index finger, held flat and horizontal so the pole can't sit in a groove.
Lay the pole on everyone's fingers and adjust until it's level and every finger touches it.
The challenge is to lower the pole to the ground. Everyone's finger must stay in contact with it the whole time. No pinching or grabbing.
It is harder than it looks: the pole tends to rise, as everybody pushes up to keep touching.
The fastest to the ground wins.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game. From a team-building night in 2018.

title: Zulu Toss
cast: A patrol in a circle · hall or field

blocks.text: Pass a ball around a circle in a set order. Then add another, and another.

items.item: Tennis ball or light ball per Scout

blocks.heading: How to play
items: The patrol stands in a circle. One Scout tosses a ball to someone across the circle, who tosses it to somebody else, and so on, until everyone has caught it once. The last Scout tosses back to the first.
Repeat until everyone knows who they receive from and who they throw to.
Start the ball again. When it is half-way round, add a second ball. Keep adding balls.
The longest time with no drops wins.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game. From a team-building night in 2018.
A silent hand-squeeze race to grab the keys, but only if a coin lands heads.

items.item: Chair per Scout, and 1 for the keys

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Put the keys on a chair at one end. Line two rows of chairs back to back leading away from the keys, with one patrol in each row, sitting and holding hands with their neighbours.
The Scout next to the keys is ready to grab. The Scout at the far end watches a leader who is holding the coin.
Nobody speaks. If they do, their patrol loses the round.
The leader tosses the coin. On heads, the far Scout squeezes the hand beside them, and the squeeze is passed along the row to the Scout at the keys, who grabs. First to grab wins.
On tails, nobody should grab. A patrol that grabs on tails loses the round.
Play first to a set number of wins.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game.

title: The Tail Wagging the Blind Dog

blocks.text: The patrol is blindfolded and linked on a rope, and only the Patrol Leader at the back can see.

items.item: Rope per patrol, or a long lashing
Blindfolds, for everyone except the PL
A course through trees, round flagpoles and so on

blocks.heading: Safety
items: Check the course. A leader walks beside the patrol and stops them if there is a hazard.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: The patrol holds a rope about 1 m apart. Everyone is blindfolded except the PL, who is at the back. The APL is at the front.
A leader directs the PL on the course with signals.
The PL calls instructions to the patrol, who must follow them, with most going to the APL at the front. Using names helps.
Set one or two courses up beforehand and time them.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game.
Carry a can of "radioactive nitro" on a board held with cords, without spilling.

items.item: Tin can, 500 mL, filled with water to 6 mm from the top
Board, 30 cm square, with a 1.8 m cord tied through each corner

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Mark point A and point B about 8 to 9 m apart.
The patrol stands around the board holding the cords. They must lift the can on the board and move it from A to B without spilling any water.
If water spills, start again.
Run it as a relay, or as a challenge to get the best time with the least water lost.

blocks.heading: Variations
items: Use a bigger can filled to 1.2 cm from the top.

blocks.text: Based on a patrol game from a Scouts program-resources list kept in Belmont Scouts' folders; the original author is not known.
Empty a bucket of "toxic waste" into a far bucket without anyone entering the danger zone.

items.item: Rope, to make a circle at least 2.5 m across
Small bucket, filled with water or balls

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Lay the rope in a circle on the ground. Put the small bucket in the middle. Put the large bucket well away. Pile the other equipment nearby.
The group has to move the waste to the large bucket using only the equipment, and without anyone entering the circle.
Allow 5 minutes to plan, then 15 to 20 to carry it out.
If someone steps inside the circle, they lose a limb or a sense for the rest of the game, for example a hand behind the back or a blindfold. If a whole person steps in, they sit out.
If the waste spills completely, talk about what went wrong, refill and try again.

blocks.heading: Tips
items: A bungee loop with cords tied on can grip the bucket from a distance, and the whole group can lift it together.
Make it harder by increasing the circle, the distance, or adding obstacles.

blocks.text: Based on an activity at Wilderdom (wilderdom.com).
Everyone must fit on a tarp that keeps getting smaller.

items.item: Tarp, blanket or circle of rope

blocks.heading: Safety
items: Check everyone is comfortable with close contact. Take off watches and dangling jewellery.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: The whole group fits on the tarp.
Fold the tarp to make it smaller, and try again. How small can you go?

blocks.heading: Variations
items: **Tarp flip:** get everyone standing on the tarp, and turn the tarp over without anyone touching the ground.
**Names:** everyone must use the name of the person they talk to.

blocks.text: Based on an activity at Wilderdom (wilderdom.com).
Line up in order of birthday, without saying a word.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Ask the patrol to line up in order of their birthdays, by month and day. Skip the year.
Nobody may talk. Expect signs, nudges and someone to take charge.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game. From Games Night, July 2023.
Pass a hula hoop all the way around a circle without anyone letting go of hands.

items.item: Hula hoop to begin, then more

blocks.heading: How to play
items: The group stands in a circle, holding hands.
Hang a hoop over one pair of joined hands.
Every person passes the hoop over their body and on to the next person, without letting go.
Add more hoops, going in different directions.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game.
Burst a balloon on the ceiling without standing up, using only the equipment you have.

items.item: Balloon, fixed to the ceiling, per patrol
Candle and matches, held by a leader

blocks.heading: Safety
items: This uses naked flame. A leader lights and holds the candle, and only older Scouts should play. Keep the balloon well away from anyone's head and hair.
If you can't do that safely, leave the candle out and use a pin on a stave.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Pin an inflated balloon to the ceiling in the middle of each patrol's area.
Each patrol sits on the floor beneath its balloon with its equipment.
The patrol must burst the balloon without anyone standing up.
The first patrol to burst their balloon wins.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game. Shared by Greg.
Get everyone across the "lava" using a limited set of blocks.

items.item: A set of blocks or mats per patrol

blocks.heading: Safety
items: Do it only on a flat, clear space. No real lava.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Mark out a river of lava between two lines.
Give each patrol a limited set of blocks, fewer than the number of Scouts, to lay a path across.
Everyone must cross without touching the lava.

blocks.text: The original notes were brief. Try it and adjust the rules.
A well-known Scout game. The version in Belmont Scouts' folders gives no author.
Sit in a circle, linked by the arms, and stand up together.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: The patrol sits in a circle with legs crossed and arms linked.
On the signal, everyone tries to stand up without breaking the circle.

blocks.text: A well-known Scout game. The version in Belmont Scouts' folders gives no author.
Send a signal to a teammate across the field, and watch them do what it says.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Split each patrol into senders and receivers, standing at least 20 m apart. The PL chooses a way to signal, such as semaphore or flags.
The first sender signals a task to the first receiver, such as "salute" or "tie a knot".
The receiver must do it. Then the next pair goes.
Keep going until every patrol member has sent and received once.

blocks.text: A well-known Scout game. The version in Belmont Scouts' folders gives no author.
Two teams get conflicting secret orders, and have to work out what to do.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Split the troop into two groups. Each sends a representative to a leader to get written orders.
The representative takes them back and reads them to the team.
On "Go", the teams try to carry out their orders.
Give orders that clash, for example one team has to leave the room while the other must not let anyone leave.
Talk afterwards about how each team handled it.

blocks.text: A well-known Scout game. The version in Belmont Scouts' folders gives no author.
A blindfolded patrol is steered into harbour by its Patrol Leader's voice.

items.item: Chairs, to make the mouth of the harbour

blocks.heading: Safety
items: Leaders walk alongside, and chairs can be swapped for cones.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: The PL stands inside the "harbour", marked by two chairs. The rest of the patrol stands blindfolded in single file, with hands on the shoulders of the person ahead.
The PL shouts directions so the ship (the patrol) reaches the harbour.
The first patrol into harbour wins.

blocks.text: A well-known Scout game. The version in Belmont Scouts' folders gives no author.
Remember where you stand, then rebuild a triangle around someone who has turned.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: All but one stand in a triangle, facing in. The remaining player stands in the middle and faces any direction.
Everyone notices where they are in relation to the middle player and their neighbours.
The middle player slowly spins, then stops without warning, facing a new direction.
The group has a set time to rebuild the triangle so it matches the new direction.

blocks.text: The original notes were hard to follow. Try it in a short round, and adjust the rules.
From a team-building games list kept in Belmont Scouts' folders; the original author is not known.
A blindfolded Scout is guided through a field of obstacles by a partner's voice.

items.item: Cones, balls and bottles, scattered over the area

blocks.heading: Safety
items: Check the space for holes and hazards, and remove them first. Leaders watch for anyone heading for trouble.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Scatter obstacles over an open space.
Pair up. One of each pair is blindfolded and cannot speak. The other guides them across with words only.
Anyone touching an obstacle starts again.
To make it harder, mark a specific route.

blocks.text: From a team-building games list kept in Belmont Scouts' folders; the original author is not known.
A reef knot tied by two Cubs who have only one hand each.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Pair the Cubs. One Cub may use only their left hand and the other only their right.
Together, they tie a reef knot in the rope.
Pairs who finish can swap hands and try again.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask afterwards
items: What did you have to do to get it done?
How might this feel for someone who has the use of only one hand?

blocks.text: A good game to talk about working together, cooperation and including everyone.
From Belmont Scouts' games folders; the original author is not known.
Learn the phonetic alphabet by saying your name in it, then play hangman with it.

blocks.heading: The phonetic alphabet
items: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India
Juliett, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo
Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Teach the Cubs the phonetic alphabet, and say it through together a few times.
Each Cub writes their name down and then says it using the phonetic words, letter by letter.
Play hangman, but use the phonetic word for each letter guessed.

blocks.text: From Belmont Scouts' games folders; the original author is not known.
Run to the compass point the leader calls, first by Six and colour, then quicker and quicker.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: The pack stands in a circle (or splits in two if there are many). A leader stands at north.
Call a point of the compass. Everyone runs to that point on the circle.
For a listening challenge, call a Six colour first, then a point: "Red Six, north-west", "Yellow Six, south-south-east". Only that Six runs.
Call faster as the numbers of those still playing go down. Spotters pick out anyone who gets it wrong.
Play to find the fastest reactions.

blocks.heading: Tips
items: Older Cubs make good callers.
A caller can point as well as call, but not necessarily in the right direction.

blocks.text: From Belmont Scouts' games folders; the original author is not known.
Draw a card with a compass point on it and run to that direction, then check yourself against the others.

items.item: Set of cards: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW
Buckets: one for cards, one for discards

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Put all the cards in one bucket. Mark the points of the compass with cones.
Each Cub draws a card and runs to that direction, either all at once on "Go" or one at a time.
When all the Cubs are at a compass point, compare to check whether everyone is correct.
Put the cards in the discard bucket and play again.

blocks.heading: Levels
items: **Silver:** four cones for north, south, east and west.
**Gold:** eight cones for all eight points. Tell the Cubs only where north is, and let them check with a compass.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game.

title: Morse Code Game
cast: Groups of four · hall or outdoors

blocks.text: Send words in Morse code across the room with a torch and decode what the other pair sends.

items.item: Game sheets with the words to send, and the Morse alphabet

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Make groups of four, in two pairs (1 and 2, 3 and 4), standing well apart, one pair at each end.
Keep the torch on. Send a signal by holding your hand across the front of the torch and taking it away: a short flash is a dot (count 1), a long flash is a dash (count 3).
Leave your hand across the torch for longer between letters (count about 5).
Cub 1 holds the torch and Cub 2 reads out the dots and dashes for each letter. At the other end, Cub 3 reads the torch flashes aloud and Cub 4 writes them down.
Carry on until the sheet is full, then decode the dots and dashes into letters to find the word.
After the first word, the pairs swap ends. Then swap roles within each pair, and send a second word.

blocks.heading: The history
items: Morse code was used in the early days of electric communication, on telegraph wires, before voices could be sent.
It was also sent by radio, and used a lot in the Second World War because it works over long distances.
Navy ships still use it, with powerful lamps, to talk to each other without being seen by others.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game.
Decode a message in which every letter has been swapped for a number.

items.item: Code sheet per Cub: a message written in numbers, with one number for each letter

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Make the code sheet. Give each letter of the alphabet its own number (use a random two-digit number), then write a line from the Law of the Jungle in numbers, word by word, leaving a space between words.
Give each Six a copy. They work as a team to find the words, looking for repeated numbers.
A good place to start is short words that keep appearing, such as THE or OF.
The first Six to decode the whole message wins.

blocks.heading: Tips
items: The classic Cub message is: "For the strength of the Pack is the Wolf, and the strength of the Wolf is the Pack."

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game.
Two Scouts hold a rope, and without letting it go, tie a clove hitch around a tree.

items.item: Tree per pair that you can walk around

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Pairs hold one end of the rope each.
On "Go", they tie a clove hitch around the tree without letting go and without passing the rope from hand to hand.
A leader checks the knot. Untie it and play again.
In a patrol with an even number, the next pair takes over the rope when the first pair finishes.

blocks.text: A Belmont Scouts game. From Games Night, July 2023.
Lash a ladder together one rung at a time, then climb it.

items.item: Long poles, for the sides of the ladder

blocks.heading: Safety
items: Test the ladder before anyone climbs. A strong ladder, an adult spotter, and only a short climb.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: The first Scout runs to the ladder and lashes one end of a rung onto a side pole, then runs back to tag the next Scout.
The next Scout lashes the other end of the rung, and so on.
When the ladder is finished, everyone runs out and holds it steady, and one Scout climbs.

blocks.text: See the Pioneering book for the lashings.
A well-known Scout game. The version in Belmont Scouts' folders gives no author.
The rules and vocabulary of improvised drama, so scenes work well and everybody has fun.

items.item: A leader as "compere", who calls the games

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Split into teams or small groups. The compere sets up a game and gives the players a situation.
Players act it out on the spot, with no script.
Use the ideas below to make scenes work.

blocks.heading: Agree to these
items: Say yes to your partner's ideas and build on them.
Don't block, ignore or deny what other actors offer.
Don't go for cheap laughs.
Be active. Do things, rather than asking questions.
Listen, and stay focused and enthusiastic.
If a scene goes nowhere, change its direction.

blocks.heading: Words to know
items: **Offer:** anything you say or do that gives another actor something to work with.
**Accepting:** taking up an offer and moving the scene forward. "Is that your car?" "Yes! Want to see how fast it goes?"
**Taking risks:** making a bold choice, like opening an imaginary car door and revving up while others make engine noises.
**Blocking:** refusing an offer, which kills the scene. "Is that your car?" "No, there's no car here." Avoid it.
**Gagging:** going for a laugh that doesn't help the scene.
**Wimping:** stalling in a way that doesn't move the scene along.

Two players act out a task, and each time the compere shouts "Freeze!", they pick up a new emotion.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Give two players a situation and a task to do together, such as washing a car.
They set the scene and start the task.
Every 30 seconds or so, the compere shouts "Freeze!". The players freeze, and the compere (or the audience) calls an emotion.
The players carry on, acting out that emotion.

blocks.text: Theatresports is an improvisation format. This version is from a handout in Belmont Scouts' folders.
Two actors speak gibberish while two translators put it into English.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Two players act out a story in made-up gibberish. Two others stand to the side as translators.
The translators say what the actors are "really" saying in English.
The actors can give the translators ideas, and the translators can steer the actors.
Build the story together.

blocks.text: Theatresports is an improvisation format. This version is from a handout in Belmont Scouts' folders.
When a scene freezes, a new player taps out an actor and starts a brand new scene.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Two players begin a scene on a given situation and relationship, such as washing a car. They work with interesting shapes and positions.
Another player calls "Freeze!" at a good moment. Both actors freeze.
The caller taps out one actor, takes their exact pose, and starts a new scene from that picture.
Carry on for several minutes so everyone gets turns.

One person sits on a bench with no character. The next person who arrives decides who they both are.

items.item: Bench or a pair of chairs

blocks.heading: How to play
items: One player sits on the bench in a park, with no character yet.
A second player arrives, decides who they are and who the person on the bench is, for example "You are a famous sports star, and I'm your biggest fan".
The player on the bench goes along with it, making the character up as they go.
The scene ends when the first player finds a good reason to leave, such as "My limo has arrived".
The second player stays and keeps their character until a third player joins to start a new scene.

title: Scene Replay
cast: Two players and an audience · hall

blocks.text: Two players perform a short scene, then do it again in a different way.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Two players perform a short scene, limited if you like to eight lines each.
The audience suggests a new way to replay it: with a certain emotion, in a different era (through the ages), in a new place, in a particular genre, or backwards.
Replay the scene each time, and see what happens.

blocks.text: Theatresports is an improvisation format. This version is from a handout in Belmont Scouts' folders.
Scenes build one by one, adding a player each time, then unwind in reverse.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: The first scene has one player, who may be given a starting situation.
The next player calls "Freeze!", steps in, makes sense of the frozen positions, and starts a new scene with two players.
Keep adding players, with each new scene starting from the frozen picture, until everybody is on stage.
Players then leave in reverse order. As each leaves, the earlier scenes continue, and the players justify their new positions as time has passed.

Act out a whole well-known story in under a minute.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: Give each group a well-known fairytale, story or movie.
They have a minute to perform it, with a beginning, middle and end and all the main characters.
They can act all the parts, use a narrator, or both.

One player types a story out loud, and others join in as the characters arrive.

blocks.heading: How to play
items: One player sits to the side and pretends to type, telling a story out loud as they type.
As characters appear in the story, other players join in and play them.
Characters can add their own dialogue to the story.
Typing noises help.
